summary: This document defines TEAP version 1, a tunnel-based EAP method that uses TLS to build a mutually authenticated tunnel. Inside it, TLV objects carry authentication and other data. It obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427.

eli5.summary: TEAP builds a private tunnel for logging into a network and exchanges credentials inside it.

subtitle: A standards-track EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel, then runs password, certificate or other logins inside it.

tldr.problem: Existing tunnel-based EAP methods such as PEAP, EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST are vendor-specific or informational, yet the industry wanted a Standards Track tunnel-based EAP method.
tldr.mechanism: TEAP first uses a TLS handshake to build a protected tunnel (Phase 1). In Phase 2 the peer and server exchange TLV objects inside the tunnel to run one or more inner authentications, then bind them to the tunnel with a cryptographic check and end with a protected result.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9930 obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427. It documents what running implementations actually do, and it states that only a small set of inner methods is known to interoperate fully.

today: RFC 9930 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7170 and updates RFC 9427, and it has not been obsoleted or updated itself. It documents TEAPv1 as implemented, and says that any fix for its known limits is left to a future TEAPv2.

sections.title: Why TEAP Exists
sections.content:
A tunnel-based EAP method is an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method that sets up a secure tunnel and then runs other EAP methods under its protection. Methods like PEAP, EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) and EAP-FAST (RFC 4851) already do this with TLS, but they are either vendor-specific or informational. RFC 6678 lists the requirements for a standard one.

TEAP version 1 is based on EAP-FAST, with largely minor changes to meet those requirements. This document defines the cryptographic derivations for TLS 1.2. When TLS 1.3 is used, the derivations in RFC 9427 MUST be used instead. The RFC notes that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated, so the definitions apply only to TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

Several implementations of RFC 7170 existed, but each interpreted the cryptographic-binding text differently. They interoperate only for a subset of the functions. This RFC describes how TEAPv1 works in theory and separately explains which subset is interoperable.
sections.eli5: Some login systems already build a private tunnel first. TEAP is the official, standard version of that idea, so different makers' devices can agree on it.

sections.title: Protocol Overview and Layers
sections.content:
After the usual EAP Identity request and response, TEAP runs in two phases. In Phase 1 it uses a TLS handshake to get an authenticated key exchange and a protected tunnel. In Phase 2 the peer and server talk inside the tunnel to set up the required authentication and authorization policies, using TLV (type-length-value) objects to carry the inner authentication, results and other data such as channel-binding information.

The architecture has four logical parts: the peer, the authenticator, the TEAP server and an Inner Method server. They may or may not be separate machines. The RFC gives the example of an IEEE 802.11 access point as the authenticator with a RADIUS server providing the TEAP and inner method components.

The outer EAP Identity SHOULD be an anonymous Network Access Identifier (NAI). TEAP packets sit inside EAP, which rides on a carrier such as EAP over LAN, RADIUS or Diameter. TLVs may appear outside the tunnel (Outer TLVs, only in the first two messages, EAP-server-to-peer and peer-to-server) or inside it (Inner TLVs, Phase 2 only).

RFC 7170 defined a Protected Access Credential (PAC) to mirror EAP-FAST. Implementation experience showed it was not necessary, so the PAC is deprecated. TEAP resumes sessions with the NewSessionTicket message from RFC 9190 instead.
sections.eli5: First you build the secret hallway, then you do the real ID check inside it. Some notes may be passed outside the hallway at the very start, but only in the first two messages.

sections.title: Phase 1: Building the Tunnel
sections.content:
The EAP server starts with a TEAP/Start packet that has the Start (S) bit set, the TEAP version and an Authority-ID TLV, with an empty TLS payload. The peer answers with TLS handshake messages and the S bit clear. Version negotiation picks the highest version both sides support. Because the version is not protected by TLS, both sides must echo it in the Crypto-Binding TLV to detect a bid-down attack.

TLS 1.2 or later MUST be used. Implementations MUST support the cipher suites TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. Cipher suites that do not provide confidentiality MUST NOT be used, and use of TLS-PSK is NOT RECOMMENDED. TLS renegotiation indications (RFC 5746) MUST be supported.

Server certificates MUST include a subjectAltName extension with a dnsName holding an FQDN, and the peer MUST normally validate the certificate, matching the realm of its NAI against that dnsName. Validation may be skipped only in listed cases, for example when the server certificate is pinned, when the peer asks for server unauthenticated provisioning, or when it is sure to use an authenticated Inner Method. The RFC says systems SHOULD prefer a private CA over public CAs.

All TEAP implementations MUST support session resumption, using either server-side state (Session ID) or client-side state (session tickets). If the server resumes the session, Phase 2 is skipped entirely. With TLS 1.3 it is RECOMMENDED to send client certificates in Phase 1 rather than via EAP-TLS in Phase 2, which saves round trips.
sections.eli5: The server says hello and shows its badge. If the badge looks real, both sides agree on a secret code and the hallway is built. Regulars can skip the full routine with a pass from last time.

sections.title: Phase 2: Inner Methods and Protected Results
sections.content:
Phase 2 follows a successful Phase 1 and MUST NOT happen if the TLS handshake fails. The server may run zero or more Inner Methods inside the tunnel, one after another, never in parallel. The inner method can be an EAP method carried in EAP-Payload TLVs, a basic username and password carried in Basic-Password-Auth-Req and Basic-Password-Auth-Resp TLVs, or a vendor-specific one. Implementations MUST support at least two sequential Inner Methods, so that both machine and user authentication can be done.

When EAP is the inner method, TEAP is simply a carrier. The server MUST NOT finish the inner EAP conversation with EAP Success or Failure. It sends an Intermediate-Result TLV instead, and a success MUST be accompanied by a Crypto-Binding TLV. Implementations SHOULD order inner methods so that a method that derives an EMSK runs first. Inner EAP methods that do not bind to the TLS session are not allowed, and tunneled methods such as PEAP, EAP-TTLS and EAP-FAST MUST NOT be used as inner methods. Resumption of inner methods like EAP-TLS is also forbidden.

A successful Phase 2 always ends with a Crypto-Binding TLV and Result TLV exchange (the protected termination). Only then does the server tear down the tunnel and send a cleartext EAP Success or Failure. A peer MUST NOT accept a cleartext EAP Success or Failure before the two sides reach a synchronized protected result. A peer that is not satisfied can ask for more with the Request-Action TLV.

A peer can also request services in the tunnel, such as certificate provisioning (PKCS#10 request, PKCS#7 reply) or channel binding. It MUST NOT request such services from a server it has not authenticated.
sections.eli5: Inside the hallway, the server may ask for one ID after another, like a door code and then a membership card. At the end both sides announce the result inside the hallway, and only then is the front door opened or shut.

sections.title: TEAP Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
A TEAP packet has Code (1 Request, 2 Response), Identifier, Length, Type (55 for TEAP), a Flags field with bits L M S O R, a 3-bit Ver field, then optional Message Length and Outer TLV Length fields, the encapsulated TLS data and any Outer TLVs. The L bit signals a four-octet Message Length (needed on the first fragment of a fragmented message), M means more fragments follow, S marks the Start message, and O signals an Outer TLV Length. Fragmentation itself follows RFC 5216 with no special handling.

Each TLV starts with a Mandatory bit (M), a Reserved bit (R), a 14-bit TLV Type and a Length. If a mandatory TLV is not supported, the receiver MUST send a NAK TLV and ignore the rest of the message. Optional unsupported TLVs can be ignored. TLVs in one packet are processed in a set order: Crypto-Binding, Intermediate-Result, Result or Request-Action, Identity-Type, then EAP-Payload (identity request) or Basic-Password-Auth-Req, then the rest.

Error TLVs carry a four-octet code: 1 to 999 are informative, 1000 to 1999 are warnings and 2000 to 2999 are fatal. A fatal Error TLV MUST come with a Result TLV indicating failure. Error 1031 (user account credentials incorrect) is NOT RECOMMENDED because it reveals valid usernames.
sections.eli5: Every message is an envelope with a few labelled boxes inside. Each box says what kind it is and how big it is, so the other side can open the ones it knows and politely say "I do not understand" about the rest.

sections.title: Crypto-Binding and Key Derivation
sections.content:
The Crypto-Binding TLV proves that the same peer and server took part in the tunnel and in every inner authentication. It also verifies the TEAP type, the negotiated version and the Outer TLVs. It carries a Version, Received-Ver, Flags, Sub-Type (0 Binding Request, 1 Binding Response), a 32-octet Nonce, and an EMSK Compound MAC and an MSK Compound MAC of 20 octets each. It MUST be validated before any Intermediate-Result or Result TLV is examined, and an invalid one is a fatal error.

The key schedule uses the PRF and MAC negotiated in TLS. In Phase 1 a session_key_seed of 40 octets is exported with the label EXPORTER: teap session key seed. For each inner method j an IMSK is taken from the EMSK if one exists (preferred), else from the MSK, else it is 32 octets of zeros. The IMSK is mixed with the previous S-IMCK to produce an IMCK, which splits into the next S-IMCK and a Compound MAC key (CMK). The Compound MAC is the first 20 octets of a MAC over the Crypto-Binding TLV (with MAC fields zeroed), the EAP type and the Outer TLVs from both first messages.

The final MSK and EMSK are each the first 64 octets of the TLS-PRF over the last S-IMCK, using the labels Session Key Generating Function and Extended Session Key Generating Function. Because inner methods may or may not give an MSK or EMSK, implementations MUST track two independent derivations, one from MSK and one from EMSK. The all-zero IMSK for password methods opens TEAP to on-path attacks, so methods without MSK or EMSK are NOT RECOMMENDED unless paired with a key-generating one.
sections.eli5: Each ID check adds a new ingredient to a secret recipe. At the end both sides cook the recipe and compare the taste. If it matches, they were the same two parties the whole time.

sections.title: Interoperability Limits of TEAPv1
sections.content:
The RFC is frank that TEAPv1 in practice does less than the protocol allows. The issue is the use and derivation of the Compound MACs: implementations derive different values when more than one inner method provides an EMSK. The most widely known TEAP supplicant supports only EAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-TLS as inner methods and does not encode, and ignores, the EMSK Compound MAC. Each authenticator implemented a different derivation, and this was found only after multiple implementations had shipped for years.

Changing TEAPv1 would leave one or more implementations non-compliant, so this document records the issues rather than fixing them. Any changes are left to a future TEAPv2. Implementations SHOULD limit inner EAP methods to a small set such as EAP-TLS and the EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2 variant of EAP-MSCHAPv2. The RFC also states that the EAP-FAST variant of MSCHAPv2 is the one that MUST be used, which swaps the first and second 16 octets of the MSK.
sections.eli5: The rulebook allows many combinations, but in real life only a few have been tested between different brands. The authors wrote down which ones work instead of changing the rules and breaking devices already in use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TEAP is designed with a focus on wireless media, where anyone can capture traffic. The tunnel gives per-packet confidentiality and integrity, user identity protection, protected inner method negotiation, acknowledged success or failure, faster reauthentication through resumption, and mitigation of offline dictionary attacks and on-path attacks. The RFC also notes that, as with many authentication protocols, denial of service by sending erroneous traffic remains possible.

The initial EAP Identity exchange is in cleartext and no intermediary should trust it. Separating the Phase 1 server from the Phase 2 server is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it risks loss of identity protection, offline dictionary attacks, lack of policy enforcement and on-path active attacks. Crypto-binding does not guarantee protection from on-path attacks if the client does not verify the server and the inner method produces no EMSK. Once Phase 2 starts, compliant implementations MUST silently discard cleartext EAP messages unless both sides have signaled a result in a protected way.

Section 8.8 admits accidental behaviors: EAP-FAST-MSCHAPv2 is used in place of EAP-MSCHAPv2, the all-zero IMSK was chosen for simplicity, and the final Crypto-Binding values might not depend on all earlier MSK and EMSK values. No analysis has been done on some of these. The RFC suggests a TEAP version 2 to address them, including a possible replay issue with the implicit EAP-MSCHAPv2 challenge.
sections.eli5: The private hallway keeps eavesdroppers out, and the final check catches anyone who tried to swap places. But the authors admit some corners are not perfect, and say a future version should tidy them up.
